## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kacchapajātaka* (Ja 178) is a story found in the Pali *Jātaka* collection, illustrating the spiritual danger of excessive clinging and attachment to one's dwelling place (*ālaya*) [Anandajoti 2010; UNDV 2009]. In the story of the present, the Buddha relates the discourse at Jetavana concerning a man who escaped the deadly "snake-wind disease" (malaria, *ahivātakaroga*) by fleeing his home [Fausböll 1879].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as a potter (*kumbhakāra*) [Fausböll 1879]. During a drought, while other creatures relocated to a permanent body of water, a tortoise refused to leave his dried-up pond due to his fierce attachment to his birthplace, thinking "here was I born, here was I nurtured" (*janittaṁ me bhavittaṁ me*) [Anandajoti 2010; UNDV 2009]. Remaining buried in the mud, he was accidentally struck and crushed by the potter's spade as the potter dug for clay [UNDV 2009; Anandajoti 2010]. Before dying, the tortoise uttered the verse preserved in the canon (verse 347), admonishing against the ruin brought about by attachment to home [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. In the identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the stubborn tortoise as a past life of Ānanda and himself as the potter [Fausböll 1879].

 Ja 178 should not be confused with other Buddhist narratives bearing the same title *Kacchapajātaka*, such as Ja 215 (the famous tale of the talkative tortoise who falls after letting go of a stick carried by geese) [Fausböll 1879] or the distinct *Kacchapa Jātaka* preserved in the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* [Jones 1952].
